newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: FEATURE - Central Asia's old Silk Road carries deadly drugs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Central Asia's old Silk Road carries deadly drugs.

text.p: The great Silk Road once saw camel caravans bearing tea, textiles and spices to Europe through Central Asia's steppe and desert.
Today it is a major smuggling route for deadly drugs, mostly opium from the poppy fields of war-torn Afghanistan.

For drug traffickers seeking to reach lucrative Russian and European markets, the highway from Khorog, near the Afghan-Tajik border, to Osh in the former Soviet republic of Kyrgyzstan is an increasingly attractive gateway.

Ill-equipped border controls pose no serious obstacle on the main road, while hardy nomads with unknown loads travel unnoticed through numerous Pamir Mountain passes in a region known as "the roof of the world".

Kyrgyzstan, a poor country sandwiched between Tajikistan and China to the south, Uzbekistan to the west and Kazakhstan to the north, has called for international help to combat an upsurge in the narcotics business that is feeding organised crime.

"You have seen the border with Kazakhstan," Interior Minister Omurbek Kuttuev told a United Nations delegation in the capital Bishkek. "There is only one border post, nothing else, and the other borders are no better.
"We have no tight border with Tajikistan and recently the frontier between Tajikistan and Afghanistan has been virtually open to anyone," he said.
The opium trail enters Kyrgyzstan from the lawless Tajik mountain region of Gorno-Badakshan, an Islamic rebel bastion beyond the control of the Tajik central government.

Ironically, the highway to Osh is known as the "road of life", for it is Gorno-Badakshan's only link with the outside world. The impoverished region depends on Kyrgyz food supplies and drugs are often the only way to get cash for payment.
Vincent Del Buono, a U.N. crime expert, told Reuters the mountains were extremely difficult to patrol and drugs were making their way through "to everywhere".
"The U.N. Drug Control Programme is actively involved in efforts to control this," he said.

But the Kyrgyz authorities, while welcoming the international aid received so far, say more is needed as the local "narco-mafia" becomes increasingly sophisticated and develops ties with Kazakh and Russian groups.
"We don't have enough of anything. We are working on sheer enthusiasm at the moment. We have to improve our equipment," said First Deputy Interior Minister Aalybay Kaipov.
He was clearly frustrated at the lack of more substantial material support from international organisations who have visited the region several times in recent years.
"They say they want to help. Then they leave," he said.
In the mountains to the south of Osh, helicopters might be the only way to monitor the frontier but the region's border guards have little more than their intuition to help them.
Russian and Kyrgyz border posts are located deep in the Pamir mountains near Kyzyl Art, where winter temperatures fall to minus 40 degrees Celsius (same Fahrenheit).

At an altitude of more than 4,000 metres (13,000 feet), sniffer dogs are ineffective and the slow search process mainly involves tapping the panels of cars and trucks, dismantling engines and wheels and poking around with a long wire.

Kaipov said the opium from Afghanistan started to appear three or four years ago, with the smuggling thriving as neighbouring Tajikistan plunged into civil war and chaos. More recently, heroin has started showing up.
"For people in Gorno-Badakshan, drugs are the only means of existence. They have taken the place of money as a currency."

Kaipov estimated that only a tenth of the amount which enters Kyrgyzstan is confiscated. About two tonnes of opium seized since 1991 is stacked in sacks in a vault at the interior ministry headquarters in Osh.

Ministry figures show that about 950 kg (2,100 lb) of all kinds of drugs were confiscated by police in the first eight months of this year. In the same period last year, only about 500 kg (1,100 lb) were seized.
Kaipov said most of the drugs came along the Osh-Khorog highway and there was evidence to show that much had reached Russia and even Europe. It was impossible to estimate the quantity.
The effect in Kyrgyzstan has been an explosion in the number of drug-related crimes from 904 in 1990 to 2,623 last year.
"Demand for drugs is growing. It is an endless fight and we must change our methods of working," Kaipov said. "We have to deal a massive blow to the source of the drugs.
"We need to influence the Afghan government and we have to get international backing," he said. "If there was one power in Afghanistan it would be possible to settle this question."
Timur Issakov, deputy head of the Kyrgyz Interior Ministry's anti-drug department, said the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 had contributed to the problem.
"It was not clear who the borders belonged to and who was responsible for them," he said. "A corridor was gradually formed."
